Introduction and meaning
Unlawful compulsory labour. Historical concordance: IPC 374. For conduct governed by the BNS, cite BNS section 146; the IPC reference is historical concordance.
In student language: BNS s. 146 is the rule on “Unlawful compulsory labour”. The section provides that whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 146 exists so that “Unlawful compulsory labour” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
146. Whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both



OF OFFENCES AGAINST THE STATE

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both
3. OF OFFENCES AGAINST THE STATE

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 146 (Unlawful compulsory labour) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 146 (Unlawful compulsory labour), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both
   (2) CHAPTER VII - OF OFFENCES AGAINST THE STATE
   (3) OF OFFENCES AGAINST THE STATE
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 146 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 146 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

learningObjectives: Master the offence of unlawful compulsory labour under BNS s. 146.
Understand the constitutional prohibition against forced labor (begar) under Article 23.
Analyze the essential elements: compelling any person to labour against their will, unlawfully.
Examine the punishment: imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both.
Appreciate the consolidation of old IPC s. 374.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 146 penalizes whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Enforces the constitutional guarantee against forced labor by criminalizing the unlawful coercion of any individual to work against their free will.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 146 (corresponding to IPC s. 374).
Actus reus: Compelling any person to labour.
Condition 1: Against the will of that person (non-voluntary / coerced).
Punishment: Imprisonment of either description extending up to one year, or fine, or both.
Constitutional alignment: Directly implements the prohibition against forced labor (begar) under Article 23 of the Constitution.
essentialIngredients: The accused compelled a person to labour.
The labour was compelled against the will of that person.
The compulsion was unlawful (not sanctioned by law, such as lawful prison labor or public service).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 146 carries forward IPC 374, serving as the general criminal law enforcement mechanism for Article 23(1) of the Constitution of India, which prohibits 'begar' and other similar forms of forced labor. Under the landmark jurisprudence of the Supreme Court (People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India), forced labor includes not only physical force or imprisonment, but also economic compulsion where workers are paid less than the statutory minimum wage or compelled to work under debt bondage. The term 'unlawfully' is crucial: it excludes legally mandated compulsory labor, such as lawful hard labor sentences imposed on convicted prisoners by courts, or statutory public service obligations imposed during national emergencies. Unlawfully compelling someone to work carries imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both.
examples: Teaching example (Confining brick kiln workers): A brick kiln owner physically locks the compound gates at night and posts armed guards to prevent workers from leaving, forcing them to work eighteen hours a day to pay off ancestral debts. This is unlawful compulsory labour under s. 146.

Teaching example (Lawful prison labour excluded): A convicted felon serving rigorous imprisonment is assigned to hard labour in the prison carpentry workshop. The compulsion is authorized by law; s. 146 does not apply.
distinctions: Section 146 vs Section 145 (Slavery): Section 146 covers compelling forced work (up to 1 year); Section 145 covers the full chattel ownership and habitual buying/selling of human beings (up to life imprisonment).

Section 146 vs Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976: Section 146 is a general penal code misdemeanor; the Bonded Labour Act provides specialized investigative, release, and debt-liquidation procedures.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a contractor who seized the identity cards and mobile phones of migrant construction laborers and threatened them with violence if they refused to work overtime without pay is guilty under s. 146.
Rule: Unlawfully compelling any person to labour against their will constitutes an offence under BNS s. 146.
Application: Physical threats and confiscation of documents were used unlawfully to compel non-consensual labor.
Conclusion: The contractor is guilty under BNS s. 146.

shortAnswer: State BNS s. 146 definition and IPC s. 374 correspondence.
State essential ingredients: unlawfully compelling labour against the will of the person.
State punishment: up to 1 year imprisonment, fine, or both.

Meaning of 'unlawfully' and lawful exceptions (prison labour).
The doctrine of economic compulsion from Asiad Workers case.

The boundary between civil contractual breach and criminal compulsory labour.

Problem scenario resolution and concluding summary.

keyTakeaways: Penalizes unlawfully compelling any person to labour against their will.
Direct statutory counterpart to Article 23 constitutional prohibition on forced labor.
Excludes legally authorized labor such as lawful prison sentences.
Punishable with imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both.
